title: Conjecture 1.1 (Pardey–Rautenbach)
statement_text: For all integers $k\geq 2$ and $t\geq 1$, every colour-balanced $k$-edge-coloured $K_{2kt}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_{c}(M)=O(k^{2})$.
context_text: Pardey and Rautenbach posed this conjecture after showing that colour-balanced perfect matchings need not always exist; the quantity $f_c(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\,|c^{-1}(i)\cap M|-t\,|$ measures total deviation from colour-balance. Prior to this paper, the best uniform bound was $f_c(M)\leq 4^{k^2}$ due to Hollom.
paper_contribution: Fully resolves the conjecture by proving that every colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2n}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_c(M)=O(k^2)$, via a linear relaxation and necklace-splitting argument.

title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: For all positive integers $k$ and $t$, every colour-balanced $k$-edge-coloured $K_{kt,kt}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_c(M)=O(\sqrt{k})$.
context_text: A $k$-edge-colouring $c:E(G)\to[k]$ is colour-balanced if all colour classes have the same size. For a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ or of $K_{kt,kt}$ (where a perfect matching has $kt$ edges), $f_c(M)=\sum_{i=1}^k\big||c^{-1}(i)\cap M|-t\big|$ measures how far a perfect matching $M$ is from being colour-balanced. More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. The authors prove, via a linear relaxation and a necklace-splitting argument, that $K_{n,n}$ always has a perfect matching $M$ with $f_h(M)=O(k^2)$, and deduce $O(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ (resolving a conjecture of Pardey and Rautenbach), $O(\Delta^2k^2\sqrt{\log2\Delta})$ for copies of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ in $K_n$, $O(\Delta k^2)$ for spanning forests, and $O_r(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of complete $r$-uniform hypergraphs. Conversely, for infinitely many pairs $(k,t)$ there are colour-balanced $k$-edge-colourings of $K_{kt,kt}$ in which every perfect matching has $f_c(M)\ge\sqrt{k/2}$, and the authors conjecture that this lower bound is the right order for colour-balanced matchings. Any improvement of the $k^2$ bound for $K_{n,n}$ would improve all their other results by the same factor. For $k=n$ a colour-balanced perfect matching is a rainbow one, related to Latin square transversals.

title: Conjecture 6.2
statement_text: There exists some absolute constant $C$ such that for all positive integers $k$ and $t$, every colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_{c}(M)<C$.
context_text: A $k$-edge-colouring $c:E(G)\to[k]$ is colour-balanced if all colour classes have the same size. For a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ or of $K_{kt,kt}$ (where a perfect matching has $kt$ edges), $f_c(M)=\sum_{i=1}^k\big||c^{-1}(i)\cap M|-t\big|$ measures how far a perfect matching $M$ is from being colour-balanced. The authors prove, via a linear relaxation and a necklace-splitting argument, that $K_{n,n}$ always has a perfect matching $M$ with $f_h(M)=O(k^2)$, and deduce $O(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ (resolving a conjecture of Pardey and Rautenbach), $O(\Delta^2k^2\sqrt{\log2\Delta})$ for copies of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ in $K_n$, $O(\Delta k^2)$ for spanning forests, and $O_r(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of complete $r$-uniform hypergraphs. For every $k\ge3$ and $t\ge1$ the authors construct a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ with no colour-balanced perfect matching (previously only one $3$-coloured $K_6$ example, by Pardey and Rautenbach, was known), which gives a constant lower bound; they conjecture that a constant upper bound holds. Since for $K_{kt,kt}$ there are colourings forcing $f_c(M)\ge\sqrt{k/2}$, the approach through complete bipartite graphs cannot prove this, and new ideas would be needed.

title: Problem 6.3
statement_text: Improve the bounds on $f_{h}(F)$ for bounded-degree spanning forests $F$ in complete graphs when $k\geq 3$.
context_text: More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. The authors prove that for every $n$-vertex forest $F$ of maximum degree $\Delta$ and every such $h$, $K_n$ contains a copy $F'$ of $F$ with $f_h(F')=O(\Delta k^2)$, showing that the error stays linear in $\Delta$ for $k\ge3$ (the first bound for forests with more than $2$ colours), but they made no effort to optimise the coefficient. For $k=2$ colours, Hollom, Mond and Portier obtained the bound $\frac{\Delta}{2}+18$, tight up to the additive constant.

title: Problem 6.4
statement_text: Improve the bounds on $f_{h}(H)$ for a Hamilton cycle $H$ in complete or complete bipartite graphs.
context_text: More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. Since a Hamilton cycle has maximum degree $2$, the authors' general bound for bounded-degree spanning subgraphs gives a Hamilton cycle $H'$ in $K_n$ with $f_h(H')=O(k^2)$, and their methods give the same bound in complete bipartite graphs. Given an almost representative Hamilton cycle with error $\varepsilon$, a necklace-splitting argument (Alon's necklace theorem) yields an almost representative perfect matching with error $\varepsilon+O(k)$; hence any improvement of the $k^2$ bound for Hamilton cycles improves the bound for perfect matchings, for which the best lower bound in $K_{kt,kt}$ is $\sqrt{k/2}$ and only a constant in $K_{2kt}$.
